newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU opens full probe into Guinness/GrandMet merger.
newsitem.headline: EU opens full probe into Guinness/GrandMet merger.

text.p: The European Commission said on Friday it had started a full antitrust probe into the proposed merger between Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc which would create the world's largest alcoholic drinks company.
The widely-expected statement followed an earlier request by the United States competition authority for more information on the 23.8 billion pound ($39.2 billion) merger.

The two giant British beverages and food groups announced last month they had agreed to merge into a new group called GMG Brands, bringing together brands such as Johnnie Walker and Bell's whisky, Gordon's Gin, Smirnoff Vodka, Guinness's traditional stout, the Burger King fast-food chain and Haagen-Daz ice-cream.
Guinness said it expected the deal to get regulatory approval.
"We are confident it will go through at the end of the year and we're watching the developments with interest," a company spokesman said.
While the United States did not disclose any investigation details, the Commission said clearly it was concerned about the new group's strong clout on the whisky, gin and vodka markets.

"The Commission has found that the merged entity would result in significant overlaps, with combined market shares of over 40 percent in the whisky sector in certain European national markets," it said in a statement released after the London Stock Exchange had closed.
"The merger could also result in significant overlaps in white spirits, and in particular gin and vodka, in some national markets."
It added: "It cannot be excluded at this stage that the merger would give rise to a dominant position in one or more of the markets concerned."
The Commission, which was giving its preliminary views after a one-month routine probe, has now about four months to take a final decision.
Under the EU's merger control law, it can impose tough conditions and indeed ban mergers and acquisitions found to create or strengthen a dominant position in the European Union.
The Commission noted that the new company's worldwide turnover would be over twice that of its two next largest competitors, Canada's Seagram and Allied Domecq.
Seagram has publicly expressed concerns about the impact on the spirits markets.
The proposed merger is also fiercely opposed by French luxury goods group LVMH Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessy, Guinness's largest shareholder with a 14.2 percent stake.
Grand Met shares closed at 590p, down 13.5p, while Guinness stock was unchanged at 605p. In contrast, LVMH finished trading 4.79 percent up to 1531 francs.
